capability.name: Choosing and saving policy sources
capability.purpose: Pick where the user and computer policies are kept (POL file, registry, a user's registry hive, a user's Group Policy object, or the live system) and save changes back to them.

actions.name: OpenPolicyResourcesToolStripMenuItem_Click
actions.purpose: Asks where user and computer policies live and opens those sources.

actions.name: SavePoliciesToolStripMenuItem_Click
actions.purpose: Saves comments and policy settings to their sources and remembers the chosen sources.

owned.says: After the person chooses policy sources, they are opened with the opening result shown, and the view moves to the nearest visible category.
When gpt.ini does not exist, a new one is written with the General section, both extension-name lines and Version 65537.
When gpt.ini is updated and already exists, its Version number is raised by 1 for a machine source and by 65536 for a user source; if no Version line exists, it is set to 65537 (both parts at 1).

Saving writes each source's comments first, then writes a source only if it is fully writable (otherwise reported as "not writable"), then remembers the chosen source types and locations for the next start. The person sees "Success." with the user and computer outcomes, or "Saving failed!" with the reason.

Saving a local Group Policy source writes the Registry.pol file, raises the gpt.ini version, and then, on Windows editions that list as having Group Policy (decided by a fixed list of product edition codes), asks Windows to refresh policy ("saved to disk and invoked policy refresh"). On other editions, the difference between the file as last on disk (read at the moment of saving) and the new content is applied to the running account's own registry (the current user's for a user source, the machine's for a machine source) and all windows are notified ("saved to disk and applied diff to Registry").
Saving a per-user GPO writes its Registry.pol file, raises its gpt.ini version and asks Windows to refresh user policy ("saved to disk and invoked policy refresh").

Saving a POL file source writes the file only ("saved to disk"); a registry source reports "already applied" because it was changed live; a user hive reports "will apply when policy source is closed"; Scratch space reports "discarded".
When gpt.ini is updated, the Machine and User extension-name lines for the registry policy are added if missing and left untouched if present.

When comments are saved, each comment gets its own text id built from the policy's namespace, policy name and a running number, and each distinct namespace gets a prefix made from its name (dots turned into underscores) and the running number.
Saving comments writes every comment and text held in memory into the target file, in schema version 1.0, replacing what the file held before.
A source's comment list is saved to its comment file location whenever the list exists, even when empty; a source without comment support has no list and is skipped.

reliesOn.says: A category is orphaned when it has no parent among the loaded definitions although its definition names one.
A category's icon is chosen in this order: orphaned, then empty, then normal.
A Scratch space source is an empty policy store that can be changed but is never saved anywhere.
For a policy's list elements, a marked-for-deletion list counts as one deleted element, and a list that holds any values counts as a present element and cancels that deletion.
A policy's lists of on-values and off-values count as enabled or disabled evidence for each value in them that is present, using the list's own key when it names one.
A category is visible when empty categories are switched on. Otherwise it is visible only if it has at least one visible policy or one visible subcategory.

A policy is visible only if it applies to a chosen area (user, computer or both). With "Only Filtered Policies" on, it must also pass the filter for a chosen area it applies to; passing for either one is enough.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to both areas shows its common state followed by "(2)" when both match, the computer state followed by "(C)" when only the user is Not Configured, the user state followed by "(U)" when only the computer is Not Configured, and "Mixed" otherwise.
A filter on state keeps only policies whose state in the checked area is Configured (Enabled or Disabled), Not Configured, Disabled or Enabled, as chosen.
When nothing is selected, the title and support lines are hidden and the pane reads "Select an item to see its description.".

A value in a policy file counts as marked for deletion when a deletion marker names it, when the key has a clear-all marker, or when a delete-values list for the key names it, regardless of case. Entries are examined in sorted order, and a value whose name sorts after the marker is stored as present and cancels the deletion, whenever it was written and whichever marker kind came before.
Listing the values of a key in a policy file leaves out the marker entries unless the caller asks for them.
An XML attribute that is absent gives nothing.
For any other element (number, text, choice, multi-line text), a value marked for deletion counts as a deleted element and a value that is present counts as a present element.

A registry key counts as a policy key when it is one of the three policy branches (software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies, system\currentcontrolset\policies) or lies below one, regardless of case.
The live registry never reports a value as marked for deletion.

A policy with a registry value of its own counts as enabled evidence when that value holds its 'on' value, which is the number 1 when the template gives none, and as disabled evidence when it holds its 'off' value or is marked for deletion when the template gives none.
Reading a value from a policy file gives nothing when the value is absent or marked for deletion.
The source name shown in the status bar is Local GPO, Registry, File, User GPO, User hive or Scratch space, followed by the path or SID in brackets when there is one.
A value in the live registry counts as present when its key exists and, unless the value name is empty, the key lists a value of that name, regardless of case. An empty name means the key itself.

No comment of a comment file can be read when any comment's policy reference has no colon or a prefix that is not declared, its text is not written as "$(resource.<id>)", its text id is missing, or two comments resolve to the same policy.
A category appears in the tree only when it passes the visibility rule; each shown category gets an icon by its kind and carries its visible subcategories below it, and the tree is sorted.
If any element is present, the elements add their count to the enabled evidence; only when none is present do deleted elements add to the disabled evidence.

A support definition met a second time anywhere in one evaluation counts as not met, because the list of definitions seen is never emptied. Two entries that point at the same definition, with no cycle, make the second one not met.
When a number is saved to the live registry, an unsigned 32-bit or 64-bit number is converted to the signed number the registry stores with the same bits, and the key is created if missing.
With both areas shown, the comment column is empty when neither area has a comment, shows "(multiple)" when both have one, and otherwise shows the single comment.
A registry source counts as writable only when a test value can be written under Software\Policies and removed again; otherwise it is read-only.
A policy file is refused when its format version is not 1, with the message 'Unknown (newer) version of POL format'.
A policy's comment in one area is empty when that source has no comment file or holds no comment for the policy, and otherwise the saved text.
A value in a policy file counts as present only if it is stored and not marked for deletion.
A policy's state in one area reads "Enabled", "Disabled", "Not Configured" or "Unknown"; the computer source is read for the computer area and the user source for any other.
When a source is closed, a mounted user hive is unloaded and the result tells whether unloading succeeded; every other kind of source closes successfully.

A source read through the file branch covers a POL file, the local Group Policy and a per-user Group Policy, each with a Registry.pol path. An existing file is loaded; it is writable only when it can be opened for reading and writing, otherwise it can be viewed but not committed.

A support entry for a product that has versions beneath it, whether a version range or a plain entry for a parent product that is not itself chosen, counts as met when any version in its range, or a sub-product directly beneath one, is chosen. The range runs from the entry's minimum (0 if none) to its maximum (the highest version if none). A range entry never matches on its own product, and a product with no versions beneath it never matches this way.

A user hive source is mounted by loading the hive file under a fresh temporary name in the machine registry, after the backup and restore privileges are switched on. If the hive cannot be opened afterwards, the source becomes an empty, read-only scratch source instead, without telling the person.

When a policy file is read and the same key and value name occur twice, the later entry wins. Key and value names are matched without regard to letter case, and the first spelling seen is kept for saving.

When the caller asks for 'any' matching, a support definition whose logic is all-of needs every entry met, and any other definition needs one entry met. When the caller does not ask for 'any', every definition, all-of included, is met by one entry. A definition with no entries, or none met, is met only when all are required. Plain product entries are checked before nested definitions.
The category tree selection follows the category shown in the right pane.

The right pane lists the chosen category in this order: an "Up: <parent name>" row marked "Parent" when the category has a parent, then visible subcategories by name, then visible policies by name. Each policy row shows its state and its comment text.

For a selected or highlighted category the pane shows its title, "This category contains N policies and M subcategories." ("The selected category" when highlighted but not opened) and its explanation. The counts include every policy and subcategory, hidden or not.

A value counts as present when: for a deletion marker, it is marked for deletion; for a number, it exists as a whole number and equals the expected number; for text, it exists as text and equals the expected text. A value of the wrong kind is not present.
The text of a policy description is tidied for display: leading and trailing spaces are removed from every line and blank space at the end of the text is dropped.
Closing the policy sources tells the person "Cleanup did not complete fully because the loaded resources are open in other programs." when any source could not release its resources.

The comment file for a source sits beside its file: the POL file or hive path with the extension changed to .cmtx; for Local GPO or per-user GPO a file named comment.cmtx in the same folder; for the registry a file under the person's local application data folder (one for user, one for machine); Scratch space has none, so comments are unavailable.
A filter on managed policies hides preferences when managed policies are wanted, and hides managed policies when preferences are wanted.
A policy file is refused when it does not start with the 'PReg' signature, with the message 'Missing PReg signature'.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for checking whether a value will be deleted: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

When the list is rebuilt, the policy already selected is selected again and revealed only if it is still listed, that is, it sits in the category shown and passes the visibility rule; otherwise nothing is selected. Then, if the policy is in the same category and the list still has that many rows, the earlier top row is put back, so the policy is not guaranteed to stay in view.
A policy passes the filter only when it passes every active part of it.
Text read from a policy file stops at its first empty character, and a multiple-string value ends at its first empty string.

For a checkbox element: a value marked for deletion counts as one deleted element. Otherwise, each present off value (or off-list value) counts a tenth of a deleted element, and each present on value (or on-list value) counts one present element. A checkbox whose template declares no on value or on list adds no present evidence, even if it holds 1.
A policy source's writability is described as "is fully writable", "cannot be saved" (changes work in memory only) or "cannot be modified"; anything but fully writable counts as a problem.
When a policy file is read, an extra empty character after the value name, as Microsoft's documentation allows, is skipped.

For a selected policy the information pane shows its title, "(no requirements information)" when it has no support rule or "Requirements:" plus the support name, and its explanation. A notice that the policy is a preference appears only for preferences.

A source's comments are used only when it has a comment file location. The folder is created if missing; an existing file is loaded and a missing file gives no comments yet. Any failure leaves that source without comments.
A policy's icon is chosen in this order: preference, then plain when it has no configurable elements, then "extra configuration" when it has some.
A policy applies to an area when its definition declares that area; a policy declared for both applies to each.
When a policy file is saved, entries are written in alphabetical order, so a key-clearing marker is always written before the values it clears.

When the Registry.pol of a POL file source, the local Group Policy or a per-user Group Policy does not exist, it is created empty with its folder and treated as writable; a mistyped SID therefore creates a new folder and empty file under the per-user policy folder. If creation fails, an empty read-only source is used and no error is shown.
A filter on comments keeps only policies that have a non-empty comment in the checked area, or only those that have none, as chosen.
When a policy lists no supported-on information, it counts as supported only if the caller allows unlisted policies. The same applies to a support entry that names no known product.

Opening new policy sources first closes the ones already open. Unsaved changes are discarded for sources backed by a POL file (local Group Policy files, a chosen POL file, a per-user Group Policy object) and for the empty source. A registry source applies changes at once, and a user hive file is applied when it is closed, so those lose nothing.

A source is writable by default for Scratch space; for a registry source it is 'no writing' when the write test failed; for others it is 'no commit' when the file or hive could not be opened for writing.

When a view setting changes, the program moves up to the nearest visible category, drops the selected policy if the move happened or the policy is now hidden, then rebuilds the tree and list. A policy kept after the move appears in the information pane only: rebuilding the list reselects the category in the tree, which clears the selection, so its row is not highlighted.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for reading a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
A category is empty when it holds no subcategories and no policies at all, counting hidden ones.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to one area shows that area's state followed by "(C)" for computer or "(U)" for user. With a single area shown, only that area's state is shown, without a suffix.
A stored policy file value is read back as text for text and expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number for numbers, a list of strings for multiple strings, and raw bytes for every other type.

A policy is Enabled when enabled evidence exceeds disabled evidence, Disabled when disabled exceeds enabled, Not configured when there is no evidence either way, and Unclear when both are equal and above zero.

A policy is a preference, not a managed policy, when it names a registry key outside the three policy locations: software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies and system\currentcontrolset\policies.

A comment file is refused as unreadable when it has no comment-definitions section, a namespace entry without a prefix, a comment without a policy reference, a text without an id, or a repeated prefix, policy reference or text id. The comments of that source are then unavailable.
After the category tree is rebuilt from the loaded definitions, no category, policy or highlighted item is selected and the information pane shows the empty state.
When a value is deleted in the live registry and its key does not exist, nothing happens. A missing value is not an error.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for listing a key's values: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
Reading a value from the live registry gives nothing when the key is missing. Signed numbers are returned as the unsigned numbers policies use, and environment variables in text are not expanded.
A filter on products keeps only policies supported by the chosen products, honouring the options to match any product and to include policies with blank support.

After opening, if either source is not fully writable the person is told "Not all policy sources are fully writable." with the state of the user and the computer source; if both are fully writable, "Both the user and computer policy sources are loaded and writable." appears only when opening was not quiet (never at start).

A REG file cannot be used as a source for asking whether a value is present: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

A support entry for a product counts as met in two cases. The entry is not a version range and that exact product is among the chosen products. Or the product has versions beneath it, and any of those versions or their sub-products is chosen, even when the product itself is not.

When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry is saved only if it has a non-empty value name that does not start with '**'. Other marker-style entries and entries with an empty value name are skipped without notice. A saved value keeps its original letter case and type.
When a policy file is clearing a key, all values and markers under the key are dropped and a single clear-all marker is stored.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for forgetting a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

When a value is saved into a REG file, it is ignored if a source branch is set and its key lies outside that branch. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Any value already stored under that name is replaced.

When a value is deleted in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it, or if the key is already marked for removal. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Otherwise the value is recorded as deleted.

When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry starting '**deletekeys' clears each key named in its semicolon-separated list under the entry's key, using lower-case names. Clearing removes only that key's own values, not its subkeys.

When a newer policy file is applied over an older one, values the old file held and the new one dropped are forgotten in the target, but only if they sit under the three policy branches of the registry.
In the live registry, 'forgetting' a value deletes it, because the registry cannot remember a pending deletion.
When a value is forgotten in a policy file, both the value and its deletion marker are removed, so the policy reverts to not saying anything about it.

The computer counts as having the Group Policy infrastructure only when the number Windows gives for its edition equals one of 59 fixed codes in a list. The edition is asked for as Windows version 6.0, and the result of the call is not checked. When the call fails the edition stays 0, which is not in the list, so the computer counts as having none.
Clearing a key in the live registry deletes every value in it but leaves the key and its subkeys. Forgetting a key's clearance does nothing.
A multiple-string value is stored as its strings each followed by an empty character, with one more empty character closing the list.
A 64-bit number is stored in a policy file as 8 bytes, lowest byte first.

When a key is cleared in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Otherwise the key's earlier entries are replaced by a key-removal entry.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry named '**deletevalues' deletes each value in its semicolon-separated list, using lower-case names.
A 32-bit number is stored in a policy file as 4 bytes, lowest byte first.

When a value is marked for deletion in a policy file, any value or marker already held under that name is dropped first. A deletion marker holding the number 32, as Microsoft does, is added unless the value is already marked or its key is cleared.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry named '**del.' plus a value name deletes that value, using the lower-case key and value names.
When a value is set in a policy file, it replaces any value already held under that name. A deletion marker for the name is not removed.
Text stored in a policy file is written in two-byte characters followed by a closing empty character.

When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry starting '**delvals' clears the whole key, using the lower-case key name. Entries are applied in sorted order, so clear-all entries come before values. Clearing a live registry key removes only that key's own values.
A value written to a policy file is stored as text, expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number or a multiple string by its stated type. Every other type is stored as raw bytes with that type.

actions.name: CompOptionsCheckedChanged
actions.purpose: Enables the text box and browse button that belong to the chosen computer source

actions.name: UserOptionsCheckedChanged
actions.purpose: Enables the text box and browse button that belong to the chosen user source

actions.name: CompFileBrowseButton_Click
actions.purpose: Lets the person pick the computer POL file

actions.name: UserFileBrowseButton_Click
actions.purpose: Lets the person pick the user POL file

actions.name: UserBrowseRegistryButton_Click
actions.purpose: Lets the person pick a user profile whose ntuser.dat hive will be the user policy source

actions.name: OkButton_Click
actions.purpose: Creates the computer and user policy loaders from the chosen sources and closes the dialog as accepted

actions.name: UserBrowseGpoButton_Click
actions.purpose: Lets the person pick the user whose per-user Group Policy object will be the user policy source

actions.name: OpenPol_KeyDown
actions.purpose: Closes the dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed

owned.says: The registry path, POL file name and Browse button for the computer side are usable only when their own choice is selected.
The registry path, POL file name, SID and hive path boxes (and their Browse buttons) for the user side are usable only when their own choice is selected.
The file picker for a POL file accepts only '.pol' files, allows choosing a file that does not exist yet, and does not ask before an existing file is chosen.

When OK is pressed, the user source is created from the selected choice: Local GPO, Registry, POL file, per-user GPO (SID typed), user hive (file path typed), or Scratch space otherwise. If it cannot be created, the person is told "The user policy loader could not be created." followed by the reason, and the dialog stays open; the dialog closes as accepted only when both sources were created.

When OK is pressed, the computer source is created from the selected choice: Local GPO, Registry (path typed), POL file (name typed), or Scratch space when none of the others is selected. If it cannot be created, the person is told "The computer policy loader could not be created." followed by the reason, and the dialog stays open.
Pressing Escape closes the policy sources dialog as cancelled.

reliesOn.says: A registry source must start with HKCU, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKU, HKEY_USERS, HKLM or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (any case); otherwise it is refused with "The root key is not valid." A path after the root is opened, and created if missing.

The path of a policy source is fixed by its kind: Local GPO uses the Registry.pol file of the system's local Group Policy (user or machine folder) and its gpt.ini; a per-user GPO uses the folder named by the person's SID under GroupPolicyUsers; a POL file and a user hive use the path given; Scratch space has none.

actions.name: SearchButton_Click
actions.purpose: Looks up the typed account name and shows its SID

actions.name: OkButton_Click
actions.purpose: Checks the SID (looking it up from the name if needed) and closes the dialog as accepted

actions.name: OpenUserGpo_KeyUp
actions.purpose: Closes the dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed

owned.says: A name typed in the user dialog is turned into the account's security identifier (SID) on Search; if the name cannot be translated, the person is told "The name could not be translated to a SID."

When OK is pressed, the SID text must be a valid SID or the person is told "The SID is not valid. Enter a SID in the lower box, or enter a username in the top box and press Search to translate."; a valid SID is returned and the dialog closes.
When OK is pressed with a name typed but no SID, the name is looked up first, and the dialog stays open if no SID results.
Pressing Escape closes the user dialog as cancelled.

actions.name: OkButton_Click
actions.purpose: Reports the chosen profile ntuser.dat path and closes the dialog as accepted

actions.name: OpenUserRegistry_KeyUp
actions.purpose: Closes the dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed

owned.says: In the user hive dialog, OK does nothing until a folder is selected; then it returns the path C:\Users\<folder>\ntuser.dat and closes.
Pressing Escape closes the user hive dialog as cancelled.
